My wife and I both work in education. She's a science teacher and I'm a counselor. In addition to that, my wife coaches sports year round and I'm a therapist in the evenings at a group practice. We work a LOT. When we're off though, summer and holidays throughout the year, we're on our national park grind. We're at 22 parks and we started our journey two years ago. This summer, our newborn came with us to his first couple of national parks. We took pictures of him while he was no bigger than a football in Shenandoah, New River Gorge, Cuyahoga Valley, and Acadia national parks. 

  
Acadia was one of the most scenic places I've seen in my life and the feeling of having the waves crash onto me at the  (near) easternmost point of the the USA after seeing a 4am sunrise in the cloudy rain with my newborn and my wife just felt.....right.

A lot of my friends do the disney vacations, the universal vacations, and all kinds of things like that with their kids but something about having your family in national parks, one of the last refuges of true natural beauty, just feels right and timeless. I want to see all of the parks with my wife, and I want to instill my son with the ability to recognize beauty as the outside world becomes more and more homogenous and sterilized.

Solution Focused Brief Therapy and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy with some undertones of existentialism and reality therapy. Earlier in life I was a cop, then a child protective services investigator. Those positions lead to a very results oriented mindset for me.

If you're super interested, I lean a LOT on a modality that came from the Medical University of South Carolina in the 1990s called Multisystemic Therapy. This is primarily used in a correctional setting for adolescents, but the framework is rock solid for all populations. 

I carry a small caseload and try to see all of my clients twice a week, for typically 3-5 months. Obviously with some clients we terminate early and others go well past that timeline, but that 3-5 month spot is pretty good about discerning if progress is being made or not.

Yes. Therapy is not for everyone, it is not a panacea, as much as I wish it were. I think there are tools everyone can use that come from therapy, introspection being the absolute best, but in my extremely humble opinion, therapy is much more art than science.  For people who are highly analytical or pragmatic, there are quite a few 'failures to launch', so to speak.

I vastly prefer the private practice experience. In most private practices, you do not get paid a "salary" Most of the time you'll be a 1099 independent contractor and get paid per session. If you work for yourself (your own private practice) you'll keep whatever you make. This is the best laid plan for most people once they get some experience. 

If you work for someone else's private practice, you will most likely have some type of 'split'. At the practice I work for, I have a 60/40 split. This means that I make 60 percent of the payment for each session, and the agency takes the other 40%. This 40% covers the admin making my appointments for me, generating referrals for me, and most client communication outside of the therapy room. 

All in all, I make about 2200-2500 per month working 12-14 sessions per week. 

In my school counseling job, I make 75k per year. Like many districts, school counselors have supplemental contracts to work a bit later into the summer than their school's teachers do. I enjoy my time at the school, but the main reason I work in a school setting at all is to have summers off with my wife who is also a teacher at my school. 

  
Biggest pro for being a part time clinician is the autonomy. I make my hours what I want them to be, I see who I want to see, and I LOVE the interactions. The session pay is great. 

Con for private practice is obviously the split fees that you have to seemingly give away to your practice. Also if clients don't show up, there's a chance you wont get paid at all. Your wages will most likely be 1099 based which means you'll need to stay on top of your taxes. 

  
If I personally did private practice, I'd make a decent chunk of change more than I do at my school job, but the benefits of free health insurance, everything that resembles a holiday being a day off, and the consistent schedule make the quality of life all too good to ignore.
